text: NHLBI identifies plaque accumulation in major surface coronary arteries as a leading cause of coronary heart disease, and describes narrowing of arteries.
NHLBI describes arterial blockage by a clot as a mechanism for ischemic stroke.
NHLBI lists coronary heart disease or prior heart attack among conditions that can damage heart muscle and cause HFrEF.
NHLBI identifies high blood pressure among conditions that stiffen or overwork the heart and contribute to HFpEF.
NIDDK lists overweight or obesity among circumstances associated with higher likelihood of developing type 2 diabetes.
NIDDK lists limited physical activity among reported risk factors for type 2 diabetes.
NIDDK includes family history in its list of type 2 diabetes risk factors.
NIDDK explains how sustained extra calorie intake can be stored as fat and produce weight gain.
NIDDK states that not getting enough sleep is linked to weight gain.
NHLBI identifies cigarette smoking as the most common cause of COPD in the United States.
NHLBI lists long-term exposure to pollutants, dust and fumes among factors raising COPD risk.
NIDDK identifies diabetes as a common cause of CKD in adults and describes kidney filter damage from elevated blood glucose.
NIDDK identifies hypertension as a common adult CKD cause and describes damage to kidney blood vessels and filtering structures.
MedlinePlus lists family history among factors associated with increased likelihood of migraine.
MedlinePlus names brain injury among possible causes of epilepsy, while noting that the cause is often unknown.
CDC identifies weakened immunity as increasing the risk of progression to active TB disease among those already infected.
NHLBI identifies pneumococcus among common bacterial causes of pneumonia.
NHLBI lists influenza virus among viruses that can cause pneumonia.
MedlinePlus describes higher depression risk when close relatives have depression or another mental health disorder.
MedlinePlus describes trauma and stressful life events as factors that may raise risk for depression.
NCI calls tobacco smoking the most important risk factor for lung cancer.
NCI describes higher lung cancer incidence associated with radon exposure.
NIDDK states that Hashimoto's disease is the most common cause of hypothyroidism and describes autoimmune thyroid injury.
NIDDK identifies partial or complete thyroid surgery among possible causes of hypothyroidism.

Cigarette smoking promotes atherosclerotic plaque buildup by damaging cells lining blood vessels, increasing plaque accumulation, and contributing to arterial thickening and narrowing. The CDC explicitly identifies increased plaque buildup as an effect of smoking.

Tobacco smoke contributes to arterial inflammation, damages blood vessel walls, and increases the likelihood of atherosclerosis. NHLBI explains that atherosclerosis involves plaque accumulation in arteries, which progressively hardens and narrows blood vessels.

Atherosclerotic plaque accumulation in the coronary arteries is the leading cause of coronary heart disease, also known as coronary artery disease. Plaque causes coronary arteries to harden and narrow, potentially reducing or blocking blood flow to the heart muscle.

Persistent or uncontrolled high blood pressure can damage arterial walls over time. NHLBI explicitly describes hypertension-related arterial wall damage and identifies stroke and atherosclerosis among the serious complications of uncontrolled high blood pressure.

CDC identifies hypertension as a leading cause of stroke and explains that cholesterol accumulation can narrow arteries, including cerebral arteries, and contribute to stroke. However, it does not independently establish the proposed intermediate relationship Arterial wall damage → Stroke.

The American Stroke Association explains that high blood pressure damages arteries and increases susceptibility to blockage or rupture. Weakened or blocked cerebral arteries increase stroke risk. Vessel blockage can cause ischemic stroke, while rupture can cause hemorrhagic stroke.

CDC directly states that coronary artery disease can weaken heart muscle over time and may lead to heart failure. The Causes section explains that atherosclerotic plaque narrows coronary arteries and may partially or completely obstruct blood flow.

AHA explains that coronary atherosclerotic plaque can narrow arteries or rupture and produce a clot that blocks myocardial blood flow. Prolonged interruption of blood flow causes heart muscle injury or death. Damaged muscle may heal with scar tissue and leave the heart weakened with reduced pumping function.

NHLBI states that chronic conditions damaging or weakening heart muscle are major causes of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. In HFrEF the weakened left ventricle cannot pump sufficient blood. Coronary heart disease and myocardial infarction are identified as conditions that can deprive heart muscle of adequate oxygen and contribute to this outcome.

The review describes dysfunctional adipose tissue in obesity as a contributor to insulin resistance: adipocyte enlargement, pro-inflammatory immune activity, excess free fatty acids and lipotoxicity can disrupt insulin signaling and glucose homeostasis.
NIDDK explicitly lists overweight, obesity, and a large waist size among factors that increase the chance of developing insulin resistance or prediabetes.

NIDDK states that type 2 diabetes develops when the body has difficulty using insulin and the pancreas does not make enough insulin to maintain glucose balance. Insulin resistance contributes to hyperglycemia and type 2 diabetes in the context of inadequate insulin secretion.

Endotext describes insulin resistance in liver and muscle as an important pathogenic feature of type 2 diabetes; compensatory beta-cell secretion can initially maintain normal glucose, whereas inadequate beta-cell compensation permits hyperglycemia and progression to overt diabetes.

NIDDK explicitly states that high blood glucose can damage blood vessels in the kidneys and that damaged vessels do not function as well. Longer diabetes duration and elevated blood glucose increase the likelihood of kidney damage.

NIDDK defines diabetic kidney disease as kidney disease caused by diabetes. It explains that high glucose can damage renal blood vessels and impair their function, while kidney damage can reduce filtration of blood and allow waste to accumulate. Together these passages support renal vascular injury as a contributor to diabetic kidney dysfunction.

NIDDK directly states that elevated blood glucose can damage kidney filters. Progressive kidney damage can impair the removal of waste and excess fluid from blood and may allow proteins to leak into urine. Kidney disease caused by diabetes is identified as diabetic kidney disease.

NHLBI explains that inhaled substances such as pollen and mold can provoke a strong immune response in some people, producing airway inflammation. It also identifies indoor and outdoor allergens as common triggers of asthma symptoms.

NHLBI explains that airway inflammation can accompany airway swelling, narrowing, excess mucus production and tightening of surrounding muscles, making breathing more difficult. Allergens are also identified as triggers that can worsen asthma symptoms.

NHLBI directly explains that asthma flare-ups occur when airway swelling or tightening narrows the airways and makes breathing more difficult. Symptoms become substantially worse during attacks and may include coughing, chest tightness, wheezing and breathing difficulty. Inflammatory airway swelling is therefore a contributing mechanism of asthma exacerbations.

Wechsler and Wells describe cigarette smoke exposure as an inflammatory trigger in COPD. Chronic smoking increases oxidative stress, which contributes to lung inflammation. Smoke-related epithelial signaling releases cytokines and chemokines that recruit inflammatory cells, including neutrophils and macrophages, sustaining airway inflammatory responses.

The review explains that inflammatory processes contribute to mucus hypersecretion, goblet cell hyperplasia, airway remodeling and small-airway fibrosis. These pathological changes, together with epithelial and mucociliary dysfunction, increase airway resistance, air trapping and persistent airflow obstruction in COPD.

NHLBI identifies cigarette smoking as the most common cause of COPD in the United States and states that long-term tobacco smoke exposure damages the lungs and airways. The article separately describes thickened and inflamed airway walls in COPD.

NIDDK directly explains that high blood pressure can constrict and narrow blood vessels throughout the body, including the kidneys, eventually damaging and weakening them. The narrowing reduces renal blood flow.

NIDDK explains that high blood pressure can narrow and damage renal blood vessels and reduce blood flow. Damaged renal vessels may no longer function properly, impairing the kidneys' ability to remove waste and excess fluid. The article also identifies hypertension as a cause of kidney disease and describes progressive damage that can lead to kidney failure.

NIDDK states that hypertension can damage renal blood vessels and other components of the kidney filtering system. Damage to these structures can impair the kidneys' ability to remove waste and excess fluid. The page identifies high blood pressure as a common cause of chronic kidney disease.

NHLBI explains that atrial fibrillation can impair effective pumping and cause blood to pool inside the heart. Pooled blood can form abnormal intracardiac clots. This directly establishes atrial fibrillation as a contributor to intracardiac thrombus formation; the atrial location is explicitly confirmed by K054S01.

The American Heart Association explains that irregular atrial contractions during atrial fibrillation can prevent complete emptying of blood from the atria. Blood may pool within the atria and form clots, increasing the likelihood of atrial thrombus formation.

The American Heart Association explicitly explains that a clot formed in the atria may be carried from the heart to the brain, obstruct a cerebral artery and cause an embolic stroke, a subtype of ischemic stroke. This establishes embolization and cerebral arterial obstruction as the required additional events connecting an atrial thrombus with cardioembolic ischemic stroke.

NHLBI explains that ischemic stroke can occur when a blood clot blocks cerebral blood flow. A clot traveling from elsewhere in the body is classified as an embolism. The page identifies atrial fibrillation among conditions associated with stroke-producing blood clots.

The Epilepsy Foundation explains that TBI can cause cerebral contusions, hemorrhage, edema, diffuse axonal injury and brain scarring. These establish structural brain injury after trauma. The article also associates certain brain injuries with later seizures and epilepsy but does not explicitly establish the complete process of epileptogenic neural circuit remodeling.

Pease et al. explain that TBI is an initiating insult that can produce structural brain injury and trigger epileptogenesis. During the subsequent latent period, neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, neuronal injury and altered signaling can contribute to the structural reorganization of neural circuitry and formation of epileptogenic networks.

The review explains that traumatic injury-associated neuronal loss, gliosis, neuroinflammation and abnormal neural circuit reorganization can promote epileptogenesis. Altered excitation-inhibition balance and recurrent excitatory connections can increase susceptibility to spontaneous recurrent seizures. Post-traumatic epilepsy is distinguished from acute provoked seizures by delayed unprovoked seizure occurrence and high recurrence risk.

NINDS identifies traumatic brain injury and brain damage as possible causes of epilepsy. It explains that attempts by the brain to repair itself following head injury may create abnormal nerve connections capable of producing seizures. The source also discusses increased recurrence risk following seizures in people with prior structural brain problems.

Ravimohan et al. describe pulmonary tuberculosis producing destructive lung pathology through caseous necrosis, cavitation and abnormal tissue repair. Caseation destroys alveolar structures and neighbouring tissue, while subsequent healing can produce fibrosis and architectural distortion. Host inflammatory responses and matrix-degrading proteases are implicated in these processes.

The review reports persistent obstructive and restrictive lung-function abnormalities after pulmonary TB and describes associations between structural damage and impairment. Cavities are associated with lower FEV1, bronchiectasis with airflow obstruction, and extensive fibrosis is proposed as an explanation for restrictive ventilatory defects. The authors describe structural remodeling as a probable contributor to post-TB impairment.

Meghji et al. describe post-tuberculosis lung disease as encompassing residual parenchymal and airway abnormalities, including fibrosis, cavitation and bronchiectasis, alongside persistent respiratory symptoms and impaired lung function. The review reports ongoing abnormalities after completion of TB treatment and recognizes an association between residual structural pathology and post-TB respiratory limitation.

The chapter explains that resident macrophages respond to invading pathogens by releasing cytokines including TNF-alpha, IL-8 and IL-1. These signals recruit inflammatory cells such as neutrophils, cause pulmonary inflammation and increase capillary permeability, producing inflammatory exudate and alveolar congestion. The histopathology section describes fluid accumulation and neutrophilic exudate within alveoli.

NHLBI identifies pneumonia as a lung infection associated with alveoli filling with fluid or pus. The same introductory description lists coughing and trouble breathing among possible pneumonia symptoms.

The chapter directly explains that inflammatory cytokines increase leakage across the alveolar-capillary membrane, decreasing lung compliance and producing dyspnea. Its clinical presentation section independently identifies cough and shortness of breath as common symptoms of bacterial pneumonia.

NHLBI states that bacteria, viruses or fungi entering the lungs can cause infection. The immune system responds to these germs, and immune cells may cause inflammation of the alveoli. The inflammation can cause alveoli to fill with fluid and pus.
Infection-induced inflammatory mediators can activate or sensitize airway cough pathways.
Alveolar infection and inflammation with fluid or purulent material are described alongside productive cough and difficulty breathing.

NHLBI explicitly identifies stress related to work, school, relationships, finances or bereavement as increasing insomnia risk. Worrying about obtaining sufficient sleep can also increase the risk of insomnia or worsen existing insomnia.

Alvaro et al. reviewed nine independent studies, including eight longitudinal studies, examining sleep disturbances and depression or anxiety. Several studies found that insomnia or sleep problems predicted later depression or higher depression levels, while other analyses identified reverse or bidirectional relationships. The review supports a longitudinal association between insomnia or sleep disruption and later depressive outcomes.

Li et al. synthesized 34 prospective cohort studies involving 172077 participants and reported an increased risk of subsequent depression among individuals with insomnia. The pooled relative risk was 2.27 with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.89 to 2.71. Eligible depression outcomes included self-reported depressive symptom scales, clinician diagnoses and structured diagnostic interviews. These findings establish insomnia as a prospective predictor of subsequent depressive outcomes.

NCI states that tobacco products and secondhand smoke contain chemicals capable of damaging DNA. It identifies tobacco use as a cause of several cancers, including lung cancer. This directly establishes tobacco-associated cellular DNA damage in general.

NCI explains that chronic exposure to carcinogens in cigarette smoke produces genetic damage involved in multistep lung carcinogenesis. The article specifically identifies the association between cigarette smoking and DNA adduct formation in human lung tissue as evidence of tobacco-related genetic damage.

NCI explains that cancer-associated genetic changes can alter regulation of cell growth, division and programmed cell death. Accumulation of relevant changes over time can contribute to malignant transformation. The article also identifies tobacco smoke as a source of environmentally induced DNA alterations.

NCI describes lung epithelial carcinogenesis as a multistep process involving initiation, promotion and progression. The article explains that genetic damage from chronic exposure to tobacco carcinogens contributes to this process and identifies DNA adduct formation in human lung tissue as evidence of tobacco-related genetic injury. This supports lung-cell DNA injury as a contributory mechanism increasing the likelihood of lung cancer development.

NIDDK identifies Hashimoto disease as an autoimmune thyroid disorder. It explains that the immune system produces antibodies attacking the thyroid, large numbers of white blood cells accumulate in the gland, and the thyroid becomes damaged. The article also identifies the disease as autoimmune thyroiditis, supporting the inflammatory characterization of the immune-cell infiltration.

NIDDK explicitly states that autoimmune thyroid injury damages the gland and reduces its ability to produce sufficient thyroid hormones. It identifies hypothyroidism as a common consequence of Hashimoto disease and explains that many affected patients develop hypothyroidism as their disease progresses.

NIDDK identifies Hashimoto disease as the most common cause of hypothyroidism. The Hashimoto-specific passage explains that the immune system attacks the thyroid, the gland becomes inflamed, and it cannot produce sufficient thyroid hormones. This directly supports the narrower inflammation-to-reduced-hormone-production mechanism.
